Galchi Gui Grilled Hairtail

Hairtail — galchi, the silver ribbon fish — is the fish Jeju islanders grill more than any other: a meter of solid meat and no bones but the spine, salted and grilled until the silver skin blisters gold.

Korean · Easy · Serves 3–4

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant — the Jeju island classic. Hairtail — galchi, the silver ribbon fish — is the fish Jeju islanders grill more than any other: a meter of solid meat and no bones but the spine, salted and grilled until the silver skin blisters gold. It is the mackerel record's (#SF07) leaner sibling: where mackerel runs fat and needs the fermented cut beside it, hairtail runs clean and sweet, and its record runs the same cure-and-grill law at a shorter clock. The skin, gone crisp, is the delicacy — protect it with the grate discipline you learned on the mackerel.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Salt the fingers and rest them, uncovered and refrigerated, 30 minutes; pat bone-dry after. Hairtail is moister than mackerel and the drying matters even more — the skin crisps only from dry.
  • Ask the fishmonger for the silver skin left on. That skin is the record's delicacy; peeling it at the shop is losing the point before you start.
  • Fire at moderate with a cool zone, grate oiled. The fat is leaner than mackerel's — fewer flare-ups, more sticking risk — so the oiling is the insurance.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Fingers skin-down on the oiled moderate grate, 3–4 minutes undisturbed. The skin will tighten, silver going pewter, then blister gold at the edges. Checkpoint — the skin lifts clean where it crisped and stays put where it has not — work from the done end with the spatula, not all at once. The flesh at the cut ends turns opaque upward from the skin.
  2. 02
    One gentle flip, 2–3 minutes more, off the fire when the flesh at the thickest finger's center is opaque and flakes at a fork's nudge. Checkpoint — a test finger pulled apart: opaque through, sweet and firm-juicy, the spine releasing from the meat with no resistance. Hairtail's flesh is dense but delicate — it will not forgive much past this point, but it does not need to; the clock is short.
  3. 03
    Platter, sesame and scallion over, lemon beside, and the eating is handwork: lift the spine free of each finger, the meat in one or two pieces. Checkpoint — eating test: crisp skin and sweet white meat in the same bite, the soy-vinegar dip for the pieces that want brightening. If the skin is leathery instead of crisp, the finger went on wet — the drying law is the record. Chef’s Note — hairtail's silver skin carries guanine — the same shimmer chemistry as fish scales at their brightest — and it is fully edible, blistering into the closest thing a fish has to crackling. The fingers curl as the skin shrinks on the heat, which is your doneness signal written on the outside: when the edges curl upward and go gold, the flip is due.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Skin stuck and toreGrate under-oiled or flipped earlyOil fully; flip only from the crisped end
Leathery skinFingers went on wetThe uncovered rest and the second pat-dry
Dry, flaky-falling fleshOvercooked on a mackerel clock2–3 minutes on the second side, no more
Fishy, not sweetHairtail past its day (silver gone dull)Buy bright-silver; frozen-at-sea is the fallback

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Salted fingers hold 24 hours refrigerated. Cooked, 2 days — the meat lifts off the spine in clean strips for rice bowls or gimbap filling.
  • Variations: a light dusting of flour before the grill (the Busan street style) for a crisper coat at the cost of some skin's shine; the same cure on mackerel (#SF07) at a longer clock; the gochujang swipe at the end for the spicy table.
